source.title: FairNorm: Fair and Fast Graph Neural Network Training

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Applies normalization motivated by prior convergence work to graph neural networks and reports convergence results in that setting; it does not test any listed version's specific intervention or conditions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training-accuracy convergence curves comparing FairNorm with NoNorm and GraphNorm. It does not report training classification error under the listed benchmark, architecture, or recipe conditions. Its normalization is group-wise FairNorm, not batch normalization.
record.test_reason: The study uses normalization's optimization benefits and Glorot initialization while evaluating its own FairNorm method. Its results concern group-wise normalization and fairness regularizers in GNNs, not batch normalization, Fixup, or any other intervention and behavior specified by V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that FairNorm improves fairness with comparable node-classification utility and accelerates convergence relative to NoNorm. Their theoretical convergence result concerns a restricted linear GNN; the empirical result concerns FairNorm including its fairness regularizers.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a two-layer GCN for supervised node classification on graph datasets with FairNorm group-wise normalization; the listed versions concern other models, interventions, datasets, or recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and activation function vary across the six convergence plots. The text says FairNorm's convergence improvement is slightly less than GraphNorm on Pokec-z and approximately the same on Pokec-n and Recidivism.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 5.2 reports that FairNorm converges faster than NoNorm across the three graph datasets and two activations. Its convergence improvement is slightly below GraphNorm on Pokec-z and approximately equal on Pokec-n and Recidivism.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: FairNorm's group-wise normalization with fairness regularizers accelerates training-accuracy convergence in the tested two-layer GCN node-classification settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 1 claims faster linear parameter convergence with group-wise shifts than without shifts in a one-layer linear GNN, under Appendix B's assumptions and specified learning-rate choices.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Group-wise centering can improve gradient-descent convergence in the paper's restricted linear GNN learning environment.

record.problems: Convergence comparisons are presented as plots without numerical values or uncertainty estimates; the text provides a qualitative summary.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error in sufficiently large convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/100, label corruption, and model-size or regularization dependence.
Spurious minima and extra student neurons in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Training degradation with depth, identity shortcuts, and special initialization of very deep networks.
Effects of initialization on training speed, signal and gradient propagation, and trainable depth. Glorot initialization is used without comparison.
Above-threshold learning rates, transient loss growth, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence.
BatchNorm versus no BatchNorm, tolerance of higher learning rates, and Fixup versus normalized residual networks.

record.verdict_notes: The row conditions and Figure 1 panel assignments are consistent with the supplied text. The revised states concern applicability to V1–V6, not a denial of the paper's qualitative FairNorm convergence finding. These method-performance rows belong under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, random or corrupted labels, model size, and near-zero training classification error.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student networks, spurious minima, and width relative to teacher size.
Depth effects, plain networks, identity shortcuts, and the cited special initializations.
Initialization comparisons, signal or gradient propagation, and trainable depth.
Learning rates above a stability limit, curvature or sharpness, and loss behavior.
The study evaluates FairNorm group-wise normalization in GNNs, not batch normalization or Fixup in residual networks.
